title: Count of Range Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair of prefix sums directly versus a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values, counting range membership in O(log n) per prefix.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and two integers lower and upper, return the number of range sums that lie within the range [lower, upper], inclusive. A range sum, S(i, j), is the sum of nums[i] through nums[j], for i less than or equal to j.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A range sum is a difference of two prefix sums","Reduce to counting pairs of prefix sums whose difference falls within a range"],["Values can be negative, ruling out a simple sliding window","A structure that can efficiently count \"how many earlier prefix sums fall in a range,\" such as a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values"]]}

blocks.text: Every contiguous range sum S(i, j) equals prefix[j plus 1] minus prefix[i], where prefix is the running sum array. The task is to count how many such (i, j) pairs produce a difference that falls between lower and upper, inclusive.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Pairs of Milestones a Fixed Distance Apart
blocks.text: Picture markers along a number line, one for each running total as you walk through the array. Two markers, taken in order, define a "range sum," the distance between them. The task is to count how many pairs of markers are a distance apart that falls within an acceptable window.

blocks.caption: Every range sum is the difference between two prefix sums

blocks.text: The qualifying range sums are S(0,0) = -2, S(2,2) = -1, and S(0,2) = 2, giving a count of 3.
The only range sum is S(0,0) = 0, which qualifies, giving a count of 1.
Before checking every pair of positions directly, notice that every range sum reduces to the difference between two entries of a single prefix sum array.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: S(i, j) equals prefix[j plus 1] minus prefix[i], so counting range sums in [lower, upper] is the same as counting ordered pairs of prefix sums whose difference lies in that range.

Observation 2: For each prefix[j plus 1], the valid partners are every earlier prefix[i] satisfying prefix[j plus 1] minus upper is at most prefix[i], which is at most prefix[j plus 1] minus lower, a RANGE of acceptable earlier values, not a single exact one.

Observation 3: Answering "how many earlier prefix values fall within a range" quickly, as new prefixes are processed one at a time, is exactly what a Fenwick tree (or a balanced search structure) over the compressed prefix values supports.

Observation 4: Since prefix values can be large or negative, they are first compressed to ranks (their position among all the distinct prefix and prefix-shifted values that will ever be queried or inserted), so the Fenwick tree only needs indices from 1 up to the number of distinct values.

This leads to processing prefix sums one at a time, and for each one, querying a Fenwick tree over the compressed values for how many earlier prefix sums fall in the needed range, then inserting the current prefix sum for future queries.
Build the prefix sum array, then check every pair of positions directly, counting how many produce a difference within [lower, upper].

items: Build the prefix sum array from nums.
For every pair i less than j (both indices into the prefix array), compute prefix[j] minus prefix[i].
If that difference lies within [lower, upper], increment the count.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: every pair of prefix sums, checked directly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The prefix sum array is built once, turning every range sum into a single subtraction.
Every pair of prefix indices is still checked explicitly, which is where the quadratic cost comes from.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of prefix indices is examined.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sum array.

Limitation: for each new prefix value, the check against every earlier prefix value is repeated independently, when in fact "how many earlier prefixes fall in a range" can be answered incrementally as prefixes are processed one at a time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair is wasteful: as prefix values are processed left to right, the question at each step is always the same shape, "how many previously seen values fall within a specific range," which does not require re-scanning everything seen so far.

What structure answers that question efficiently: a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) that supports adding a value and querying a prefix count in O(log n), letting a RANGE count be found as one query minus another.

Why compress the values first: prefix sums, and the shifted values (prefix minus lower, prefix minus upper) used in queries, can be large or negative, so they are mapped to small positive ranks before being used as Fenwick tree indices.

The core idea: process prefix sums left to right, and for each one, query the Fenwick tree for how many earlier prefix sums fall within [current minus upper, current minus lower], then insert the current prefix sum for future queries.

Collect every prefix sum value, along with prefix sum minus lower and prefix sum minus upper for every prefix, and compress them all to ranks. Process prefix sums left to right: for each one, query the Fenwick tree for how many earlier prefix sums have rank within the needed range, add that to the count, then insert the current prefix sum's rank into the tree.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: compress prefix values to ranks, use a Fenwick tree to count range membership

blocks.text: Since S(i, j) equals prefix[j] minus prefix[i], counting qualifying range sums ending at j is exactly counting earlier prefix values falling within [prefix[j] minus upper, prefix[j] minus lower]. A Fenwick tree over the compressed prefix values supports both inserting a new prefix and querying how many fall at or below a given rank in O(log n), so a range count is just two such queries subtracted, letting the whole array be processed in O(n log n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), n Fenwick tree updates and queries, each O(log n).
Space: O(n), for the prefix sums, the compressed rank mapping, and the Fenwick tree.

items: Forgetting to include the shifted query values (prefix minus lower, prefix minus upper) when building the coordinate compression, which would make later lookups fail.
Off-by-one errors in the Fenwick tree's range query, remember a range count is query(hi) minus query(lo minus 1), not query(hi) minus query(lo).
Inserting the current prefix into the tree before querying against it, which would incorrectly count a range sum against itself.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair of prefix sums", think: process prefixes one at a time, and use a Fenwick tree over compressed values to count how many earlier ones fall in the needed range.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized Fenwick tree approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: reduce range sums to prefix sum differences, then count qualifying pairs with a Fenwick tree over compressed values.
Core Idea: process prefix sums one at a time, querying a Fenwick tree for how many earlier prefixes fall within the range needed to make the current difference qualify.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized Fenwick tree approach.
Space: O(n) for both.
Most Important Observation: every range sum is a difference of two prefix sums, turning this into a range-counting problem over a single 1D sequence of values.
Interview Difficulty: the prefix-sum reduction is standard; correctly compressing coordinates and querying a Fenwick tree range is the harder, higher-value part.
One line memory trick: range sums are prefix differences, count them with a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values.
